title: Photo sharing
brief: You are building a photo app. People post pictures and everyone else scrolls through them. Almost all the traffic is people looking at photos, and the photos take up far more room than anything else you store.

clarify.q: Do people edit a photo after posting?
clarify.a: No. A photo never changes after it is posted, only its caption and likes do. That makes photos very safe to copy near users.
Never. People treat these as memories. Once the app says "posted", the photo must survive.

clarify.q: How fast must a photo open?
clarify.a: The scored photo-read p99 target is 450 ms, including network travel. Uploads have a separate 4,000 ms target.

clarify.q: Do we keep every size of a photo?
clarify.a: Yes: the original plus a few smaller sizes. Together that is about 3 MB per photo.

notes: About 1 million photos are posted per day (approx.).
The 150 TB figure is the busy recent set, not every photo ever posted (approx.).

numbers.label: Photo views per second at peak
New photos per day
numbers.how: about 1 in 30 people post each day (approx.)

hints: Photos never change. What does that let you do with copies of them?
A CDN keeps copies of popular photos close to people, so most views never reach your own servers. Photo bytes belong in object storage, not in a database.
Try: people -> CDN -> app servers -> object storage for the photos and a SQL database for captions and likes. Put a cache in front of the database for the busy rows.

editorial.summary: Photos are big, never change and are viewed far more than they are posted. That is the perfect case for a CDN in front and cheap object storage behind. The app servers and database only handle small things: captions, likes and who follows whom.

designs.name: CDN, app servers, object storage
designs.why: The CDN answers most photo views from a nearby copy. App servers handle uploads and small writes. Object storage keeps every photo safely and cheaply. A cache protects the database from repeat questions.

designs.name: The same design with backups
designs.why: Same design, plus backups of the captions database, so a bad deploy or a deleted table can be rolled back. The photos already sit in object storage, which keeps several copies of every file.

tradeoffs: A long CDN cache time means more photo views are served from the edge and the bill is lower, but a deleted photo can stay visible for a while.
Object storage is cheap per gigabyte but slower than a disk next to your server. It is the right home for photos and the wrong home for a like counter.
Several app servers in two zones cost more than one big server, but one failed building no longer takes the app down.
A cold archive cuts the storage bill but makes a rare old-photo view slower. Most people never notice.
editorial.realWorld: Large photo apps serve well over 90 percent of photo views from CDN caches (approx.), and store petabytes of photos in cheap object storage, with each photo kept in a handful of sizes.

correctness.prompt: Photo sharing: The same request is delivered twice, and a worker can crash after saving it. What uniqueness constraint and transaction would keep one durable result?
correctness.discussion: Choose a stable business operation id and enforce a unique constraint in the authoritative store. Insert the id, apply the change and save its result in one transaction. A retry returns that result. Recording the id before the change can lose work after a crash; recording it afterwards can apply the change twice. If work continues through a queue, commit an outbox entry in the same transaction and deduplicate at each consumer.

fields.label: The server commits a change, then crashes before replying. The client retries. What happens?
options: Commit the operation id, effect and result atomically; return that result on retry
Record the id first, then apply the change in a separate write
fields.explanation: Recording the id separately can either lose an operation or apply it twice. The effect and deduplication result must commit together.

fields.label: The server acknowledges a write just before its storage fails. Which evidence meets the stated recovery point?
options: A queued backup request with no completed durable copy
A durable copy across the required failure boundary before acknowledgement
fields.explanation: A scheduled copy is not a completed copy. Match acknowledgement and recovery to the stated loss boundary.
